content.text:
I submitted **holistic** with confidence 0.5 and used the full budget of 60. The evidence leans that way but is weak, because the test noise is large compared with the differences between tasks.

**Phase 1 (trained only L1-S2-M1).** I tested two tasks that each had exactly one new rule but very different similarity to the trained task:

| Task | Similarity | Mean examples (n=4) |
|---|---|---|
| L1-S2-M3 | 0.75 | ~10 |
| L2-S2-M1 | 0.0 | ~27.5 |

With the new-rule count held equal, similarity mattered. That argues against part-based. A fully novel control (L4-S4-M4: 3 new rules, similarity 0) took about 39.

**Phase 2 (trained 9 more tasks, 10 in total).** These made L3, S3 and M3 each appear in exactly 3 trained tasks, while keeping target L3-S3-M3 at most 0.375 similar to anything trained. Part-based, and factor-when-justified with k = 2 or 3, both predict this task should be among the cheapest, since all three of its rules are reusable parts.

| Task | New rules | Similarity | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| L3-S3-M3 (target) | 0 | 0.375 | mean ~26.5 (n=12) |
| L4-S3-M4 | 1 | 0.75 | mean ~23 (n=13) |
| L1-S2-M3 | 0 | 0.75 | mean ~23 (n=4) |
| L2-S1-M4 | 2 | 0.19 | mean ~34 (n=4) |

The all-parts target was no cheaper than the high-similarity task that has a new rule, and it was slightly more expensive. That fits holistic better than either rule-based mechanism.

**Why confidence is only moderate:**
- Single results ranged widely, from 1 to 55 for the same task, and the key target-vs-L4-S3-M4 gap is only about 3–4 examples.
- L1-S2-M3 took ~10 in phase 1 but ~23 in phase 2. More training shouldn't make a task harder under any of the three hypotheses, so this points to the noise being large.
- In this task set, the number of new rules and similarity tend to move together, so I could only partly separate them. L3-S3-M3 was the only untrained task available with 0 new rules and low similarity to the trained set.
